prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: flood defences and the premium. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a property has permanent flood defences that are properly maintained and evidenced, I can usually treat the risk as lower for the next renewal review, but only if the measures match the actual local flood source rather than just surface water. "},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood resilience measures are only temporary or ad hoc, I should not assume any premium benefit unless there is clear, recent evidence that they are deployed reliably and are suitable for the expected flood type. "},{"type":"observation","content":"When a claim shows repeated water ingress despite existing defences, I should flag that the premium position may need rechecking, because the history matters as much as the hardware. "},{"type":"preference","content":"When members provide installation certificates, survey notes, or maintenance records for flood barriers, I prefer to use those documents to support a more favourable view than verbal reassurance alone. "},{"type":"observation","content":"When the property sits in a mapped flood-prone area but has raised thresholds, non-return valves, or airbrick protection, I should still distinguish between reduced severity and eliminated risk. "},{"type":"fact","content":"When defences are designed for river flooding but the event is driven by surface water or overwhelmed drainage, I should avoid over-crediting the premium because the protection may not address the main peril. "},{"type":"observation","content":"When members have recently invested in resilience after a previous claim, I should note the improvement and check whether it is reflected in the next underwriting view, rather than carrying forward the older risk profile unchanged. "},{"type":"preference","content":"When evidence is mixed, I prefer to err on the side of asking for a few precise details about the defence type, date fitted, and maintenance, because that usually gives a better premium decision than broad assumptions. "},{"type":"fact","content":"When local authority or Environment Agency-style warnings have been heeded and mitigation is in place, that can support a better assessment of future loss control, but it does not by itself justify a premium reduction. "},{"type":"observation","content":"When a home has well-kept flood doors, pump systems, and clear emergency plans, I should recognise the resilience, yet I still need to check whether the insurer’s pricing rules allow any rating change before I suggest one. "}]}
